1.q: ה֚וֹי אֲרִיאֵ֣ל אֲרִיאֵ֔ל קִרְיַ֖ת חָנָ֣ה דָוִ֑ד
1.note: Isaiah is speaking directly to the city of Jerusalem as if it could hear him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state whom he is speaking about. Alternate translation: [Woe is to Jerusalem, the city where David encamped]

Isaiah is using the word **Woe** to express his distress about what will happen to the people of Jerusalem. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Disaster is coming] or [There is danger ahead for you]

Isaiah is using the phrase **Add year to year** as a common expression of the culture to mean “year after year.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Year after year] or [Every year]

Isaiah actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not think that it will benefit you to add year to year, to let the festivals come around]

2.note: Isaiah uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the celebration described in the previous verse and the distress that Yahweh will bring upon Jerusalem. Use a natural way in your language to indicate this contrast. Alternate translation: [Although the festivals come around, I will cause distress]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But I will greatly distress Ariel]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **mourning** and **lamentation**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [and they will mourn and lament]

The terms **mourning** and **lamentation** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [deep mourning]

The point of this comparison is that just as **an altar hearth** is a place where sacrifices are consumed by fire, so Jerusalem will be a place of bloodshed and destruction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [and it will be to me a place of bloodshed and destruction, like an altar hearth]

An **altar hearth** is a kind of raised platform where animals were burned as sacrifices to God. If your readers would not be familiar with what an altar hearth is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like the place where sacrifices are burned]
The word **Ariel** means **altar hearth.** If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote.

3.note: Here and throughout verses 3-5 of this chapter, the word **you** is feminine singular because it refers to Ariel, the city of Jerusalem, personified as a woman. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the feminine form if your language marks that distinction.

The point of this comparison is that just as **a circle** completely surrounds what is inside it, so Yahweh will completely surround Jerusalem with a besieging army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [And I will encamp against you and surround you completely, as a circle surrounds what is inside it]

4.note: Isaiah is speaking as if Jerusalem’s humiliation were physically going down, as expressed by the phrase **become low**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you will be humiliated]

Isaiah is speaking as if Jerusalem’s humiliation were being brought down to **the dust**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your speech will be from a position of deep humiliation]

A **ritual pit** is a kind of hole in the ground that people used to try to summon the spirits of the dead. If your readers would not be familiar with what a ritual pit is, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like a pit used to consult the spirits of the dead]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a ritual pit** produces a faint, eerie sound from underground, so Jerusalem’s voice will be weak and ghostly after its defeat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [And your voice will sound as faint and eerie as a the sounds in a ritual pit from the earth]

Isaiah is speaking as if Jerusalem’s faint speech would **chirp** like a bird chirping from the dust. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your speech will be high-pitched but faint, from the dust]

5.note: Isaiah uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between Jerusalem’s humiliation in the previous verses and the sudden destruction of its enemies. Use a natural way in your language to indicate this contrast. Alternate translation: [However, the multitude of your strangers will be]

The point of this comparison is that just as **fine dust** is light and easily blown away, so Jerusalem’s enemies will be quickly and easily scattered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [But the multitude of your strangers will be easily blown away like fine dust]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context. Alternate translation: [and the multitude of the terrible will be like passing chaff]

Isaiah is using the adjective **terrible** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [terrible ones]

The point of this comparison is that just as **passing chaff** is blown away by the wind and disappears, so the enemies of Jerusalem will be quickly swept away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [and the multitude of the terrible will be swept away like chaff that the wind blows away]

6.note: The expression **it will be visited** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [he will strike]

Isaiah is speaking of **the flame of a devouring fire** as if it were a living thing that could consume things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a fire that burns up everything in its path]

7.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a dream** is not real and fades away when a person wakes up, so the attack of the nations against Jerusalem will vanish suddenly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [And it will suddenly vanish, just as a dream fades away when a person wakes up in the night]

Isaiah is using **a vision of the night** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a dream.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a dream during the night]

Isaiah says **all of the nations** and **all of the ones warring against it** as extreme statements for emphasis. He does not mean that literally every nation will attack Jerusalem, but rather that many nations will do so. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form of exaggeration or express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [a vast number of nations warring against Ariel and a vast number of the one warring against it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the ones bringing harm]

8.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֡ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר֩ יַחֲלֹ֨ם הָ⁠רָעֵ֜ב וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה אוֹכֵ֗ל וְ⁠הֵקִיץ֮ וְ⁠רֵיקָ֣ה נַפְשׁ⁠וֹ֒ וְ⁠כַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יַחֲלֹ֤ם הַ⁠צָּמֵא֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה שֹׁתֶ֔ה וְ⁠הֵקִיץ֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה עָיֵ֔ף וְ⁠נַפְשׁ֖⁠וֹ שׁוֹקֵקָ֑ה
8.note: These two sentences mean basically the same thing. The second clause strengthens the thought in the first clause by repeating the same idea with different words. Isaiah is emphasizing that the enemies’ hopes of conquering Jerusalem will be completely unfulfilled, just as a hungry or thirsty person’s dream of eating or drinking leaves them still unsatisfied. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could combine these clauses and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And it will be like when the hungry dreams of eating but awakens unsatisfied, or like when the thirsty dreams of drinking but awakens still faint and longing]

8.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֡ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר֩ יַחֲלֹ֨ם הָ⁠רָעֵ֜ב וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה אוֹכֵ֗ל וְ⁠הֵקִיץ֮ וְ⁠רֵיקָ֣ה נַפְשׁ⁠וֹ֒
8.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the hungry** person dreams of eating but wakes up still empty, so the nations attacking Jerusalem will find that their hopes of conquest are completely unfulfilled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [And it will be as when a hungry person dreams of eating but awakens, and his soul is still empty]

Isaiah is using the adjective **hungry** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a person who is hungry]

Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look, he is eating]
Here, **his soul** represents “the person himself.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he himself is empty]

8.q: וְ⁠כַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יַחֲלֹ֤ם הַ⁠צָּמֵא֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה שֹׁתֶ֔ה וְ⁠הֵקִיץ֙ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה עָיֵ֔ף וְ⁠נַפְשׁ֖⁠וֹ שׁוֹקֵקָ֑ה
8.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the thirsty** person dreams of drinking but wakes up still longing for water, so the nations attacking Jerusalem will find their ambitions completely unfulfilled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [Or like a thirsty person who dreams of drinking but wakes up still faint, his longing unsatisfied]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply these words from the context. Alternate translation: [Or it will be like when the thirsty person dreams]

Isaiah is using the adjective **thirsty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a thirsty person]

Here, **his soul** represents “the person himself.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he himself is longing]

8.q: הֲמוֹן֙ כָּל הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֔ם הַ⁠צֹּבְאִ֖ים עַל הַ֥ר צִיּֽוֹן
8.note: Isaiah says **all of the nations** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He does not mean that literally every nation will war against Mount Zion, but rather that many nations will do so. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form of exaggeration or express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [the vast multitude of nations warring against Mount Zion]

9.note: Isaiah actually means to communicate the opposite of what he is saying. He is not truly commanding the people to blind themselves and be amazed. Rather, he is condemning them for their willful refusal to understand. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You stubbornly refuse to understand, and you have blinded yourselves]

The word translated as **Make yourselves wait** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Scholars have proposed that the original form may have been a similar word that means “Be amazed.” That would seem to fit the meaning of this passage better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [Be amazed and have amazement]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **amazement**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and be amazed]

9.q: שָֽׁכְר֣וּ וְ⁠לֹא יַ֔יִן נָע֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א שֵׁכָֽר
9.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the people’s spiritual stupor were them being **drunk** on wine and staggering from beer. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They are confused and disoriented, but not because of wine or beer]

The pronoun **They** refers to the same people whom Isaiah was addressing with the commands in the first part of the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people of Jerusalem are drunk]

10.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Isaiah is speaking as if spiritual blindness were **a spirit of deep sleep** that could be **poured out** like liquid. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has made you completely unable to understand]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **a spirit** that is characterized by **deep sleep**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a spirit that causes deep sleep]

Isaiah is speaking as if preventing understanding were Yahweh having **closed your eyes**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he closed the understanding of the prophets]

Isaiah is speaking as if the prophets were the **eyes** of the nation, since prophets enable the people to perceive spiritual truth just as eyes enable a person to see. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your eyes, the prophets, those who enable you to perceive spiritual truth]

Isaiah is speaking as if preventing the seers from receiving visions were having **covered your heads**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he has prevented the seers from seeing]

Isaiah is speaking as if the seers were the **heads** of the nation, since seers guide the people spiritually just as the head directs the body. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your leaders, the seers]

11.note: The expression **a sealed scroll** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a scroll that a person sealed]

Isaiah is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone gives it to one knowing writing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vision**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all that the prophets have seen]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the words of a sealed scroll** cannot be read because the scroll is closed, so the prophetic vision cannot be understood because Yahweh has made the people unable to comprehend it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point of comparison explicit. Alternate translation: [like the words of a sealed scroll that no one can understand]

The expression **sealed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a scroll someone sealed]

12.note: The expression **the scroll is given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Or someone gives the scroll]

13.note: Here, **its mouth** represents “what they say.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [this people approaches with their words]

13.q: בְּ⁠פִ֤י⁠ו וּ⁠בִ⁠שְׂפָתָי⁠ו֙ כִּבְּד֔וּ⁠נִי וְ⁠לִבּ֖⁠וֹ רִחַ֣ק מִמֶּ֑⁠נִּי וַ⁠תְּהִ֤י יִרְאָתָ⁠ם֙
13.note: The pronouns **its** and **their** refer to the collective **people** mentioned earlier in the verse. Isaiah shifts between singular and plural forms because he is treating the people both as a single group and as individuals. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [with the people’s mouth and they honor me with the people’s lips, but the people’s heart is far from me and their fearing of]

Here, **its lips** represents “what they say.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they honor me with what they say]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s lack of true devotion were their **heart** being physically **far** from him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but inwardly they are not devoted to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fearing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way they fear me]

The expression **a taught commandment** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a commandment that men have taught them]

14.note: The word translated as **therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [for that reason]

Yahweh is using **behold me, one will add** as a common expression of this culture to mean “I am going to add.” Someone using this expression would more commonly say “Behold me, adding.” Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making a solemn pronouncement. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in 28:16. Alternate translation: [I am surely going to add]

14.q: הַפְלֵ֣א וָ⁠פֶ֑לֶא וְ⁠אָֽבְדָה֙ חָכְמַ֣ת חֲכָמָ֔י⁠ו וּ⁠בִינַ֥ת נְבֹנָ֖י⁠ו
14.note: This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonder**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and something that astonishes them]

Isaiah is speaking of **wisdom** as if it were a living thing that could **perish**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And its wise people will no longer be wise]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what its wise people know]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **understanding**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what its discerning people know]

Isaiah is repeating forms of the word **wonderful** in order to intensify the idea. If your language does not use repetition for this purpose, you could use one form and express the intensity in another way. Alternate translation: [doing something truly wonderful]

Isaiah is speaking of **understanding** as if it were a living thing that could **hide itself**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the understanding of its intelligent ones will disappear]

15.note: Isaiah is using **Woe to** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Warning of coming judgment upon.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [There will be great trouble for]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they plan to do]

Isaiah is speaking as if the people’s secret schemes were being done **in darkness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their deeds are done in secret]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **darkness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in dark places]

Isaiah is using the question form for emphasis to show that the people believe no one can see their secret plans. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one can see us, and no one can know about us!]

16.note: Isaiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, that of indignation at the people’s audacity in reversing the proper relationship between God and his creatures. If your language uses exclamations to express such feelings, it would be appropriate to use one here. Alternate translation: [How you have turned everything upside down!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **overturning**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How you turn things upside down]

16.q: אִם־כְּ⁠חֹ֥מֶר הַ⁠יֹּצֵ֖ר יֵֽחָשֵׁ֑ב כִּֽי־יֹאמַ֨ר מַעֲשֶׂ֤ה לְ⁠עֹשֵׂ֨⁠הוּ֙ לֹ֣א עָשָׂ֔⁠נִי וְ⁠יֵ֛צֶר אָמַ֥ר לְ⁠יוֹצְר֖⁠וֹ לֹ֥א הֵבִֽין
16.note: Isaiah is using the question form for emphasis to show the absurdity of people treating God as if they were equal to him, just as it would be absurd for a potter to be considered as equal to the clay. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is absurd that the potter should be regarded as the clay, that the made should say of its Maker, “He did not make me,” or the form should say of its Former, “He does not understand”!]

16.q: אִם־כְּ⁠חֹ֥מֶר הַ⁠יֹּצֵ֖ר יֵֽחָשֵׁ֑ב כִּֽי־יֹאמַ֨ר מַעֲשֶׂ֤ה לְ⁠עֹשֵׂ֨⁠הוּ֙ לֹ֣א עָשָׂ֔⁠נִי וְ⁠יֵ֛צֶר אָמַ֥ר לְ⁠יוֹצְר֖⁠וֹ לֹ֥א הֵבִֽין
16.note: See how you translated the similar expressions beginning with “As if” in 10:15. Alternate translation: [The potter should certainly not be regarded as the clay! The made should certainly not say of its Maker, “He did not make me”! And the form should certainly not say of its Former, “He does not understand”!]

The expression **should be regarded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you should regard the potter as the clay]

Isaiah is speaking as if the relationship between God and his people were the relationship between **the potter** and **the clay**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Creator should be regarded as one of his creatures]

Isaiah is speaking of **the make** as if it were a living thing that could speak and deny its Maker. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the thing made should say of its Maker, “He did not make me,”]

Isaiah is speaking of **the form** as if it were a living thing that could speak and accuse its Former of lacking understanding. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [or a person should say of the one who formed him, “He does not understand what he was doing”]

17.note: The terms **a little** and **a trifle** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a very little while]

17.q: הֲ⁠לוֹא עוֹד֙ מְעַ֣ט מִזְעָ֔ר וְ⁠שָׁ֥ב לְבָנ֖וֹן לַ⁠כַּרְמֶ֑ל וְ⁠הַ⁠כַּרְמֶ֖ל לַ⁠יַּ֥עַר יֵחָשֵֽׁב
17.note: Isaiah is using the question form for emphasis to assert that the coming reversal will happen very soon. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [In just a very short time, Lebanon will turn into agricultural land, and agricultural land will be regarded as a forest.]

The expression **will be regarded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will regard agricultural land as a forest]

18.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **on that day** to introduce a new event in the prophecy. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. See the UST.

Isaiah is using the adjective **deaf** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are deaf]

Isaiah is speaking as if the people’s lack of spiritual understanding were **gloom** and **darkness** from which they could emerge to **see**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and those who lacked spiritual understanding will come to understand]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gloom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and from dim places]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **darkness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and from dark places]

Isaiah is using the adjective **blind** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are blind]

19.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rejoicing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [great joy]

Isaiah is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are poor]

Isaiah is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and the poor among people]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **the Holy One** who is worshiped by **Israel**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the Holy One whom Israel worships]

20.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This will happen because]

Isaiah is using the adjective **terrible** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. See how you translated the similar expression in 29:5. Your language may use adjectives in the same way.
